A colleague at Suvanto mentioned your SAR antenna development over coffee last month, and I went home and read everything I could find about Kaikuvaara’s instrument programmes for airborne and spaceborne remote sensing. Sami Korhonen

Building measurement instruments that need to function correctly on the first attempt — in orbit, where there is no second try — is what I want to be doing for the remaining years of my career. When I saw Kaikuvaara’s posting for a Senior Signal Processing Engineer, it was the first job listing in a long time that genuinely aligned with that ambition, and I felt it was worth reaching out.

I have spent most of my career at Polaris RF Labs here in Oulu, where I work on algorithm design and simulation for ground-based communications receiver systems. My core focus has been spectral estimation, interference mitigation, and adaptive filtering, working primarily in MATLAB and Simulink. The work is analytical rather than implementation-heavy: I design and verify algorithms at the system level, write the specifications, and hand them to the implementation team for deployment. Over the past several years my interest has shifted increasingly toward spatial processing, and I was responsible for the beamforming algorithm design on Polaris’s 8-element adaptive receiver prototype. That project involved computing real-time steering weights under co-channel interference and designing the calibration routine for gain and phase errors across the array elements. It was the first time I worked directly with a phased-array architecture rather than modelling one from a distance, and it changed the direction of what I want to do. Array signal processing, and specifically the kind of precision beamforming work that Kaikuvaara does for remote-sensing instruments, is where I want to put my effort going forward.

My degree is an MSc in Engineering Physics from Gotaalv University of Technology in Gothenburg, completed in 1999. The programme’s emphasis was on electromagnetic theory, mathematical physics, linear systems, and numerical methods — a curriculum oriented around principles rather than specific applications. That depth has paid off many times: when a design problem resists the textbook approach, I fall back on the physics-based framework I learned there and it rarely lets me down.

All of my professional work at Polaris has involved regular technical interaction with English-speaking partners and customers. For extended periods, including a multi-year collaboration with a UK-based systems integrator, the working language was entirely English. I am fully comfortable with technical writing, presentations, and daily communication in English.

I recognise that twenty-plus years at a single employer might read as a narrow profile. I see it differently: I stayed because the problems held my attention, and now I want to go where they are harder. I took a sabbatical in 2002–03 to travel and returned with a clearer sense of what I valued in work. The algorithmic experience I have built at Polaris transfers to Kaikuvaara’s instrument challenges more directly than the job titles might suggest.

I am in Oulu already, so relocation is not a factor. Happy to discuss at your convenience.

Antti Rantanen

Dear Hiring Manager,

I am writing to apply for the Senior Signal Processing Engineer position at Kaikuvaara Oy. I have followed Kaikuvaara’s work in remote-sensing instrumentation for some years now, and the company’s place within Oulu’s RF and photonics engineering community is a significant part of what draws me to this role. The concentration of wireless, radar, and space-systems expertise in the region is unusual in Europe, and the prospect of working alongside the research groups, Suvanto, and the cluster of instrument companies in the area is professionally attractive in a way that few other Nordic locations can match.

I have spent the past nineteen years at Nordkom Radar Systems, where my work has covered most of the signal-processing chain from algorithm design through to delivered flight hardware. The project I am most proud of is the digital beamforming pipeline I designed for a 64-element L-band phased-array receiver built for a maritime surveillance radar. I was responsible for the entire receive path: spatial sampling, per-element gain and phase correction, subarray summation, and adaptive null steering. The array’s wide scan-angle requirement demanded careful grating-lobe suppression and mutual-coupling compensation across the full steering range. Taking that design from a MATLAB proof-of-concept through to a working receiver that met its sidelobe specification against measured sea-clutter data was the most complete piece of systems engineering I have done.

A large part of the same programme required embedded real-time implementation. I wrote the pulse-compression and Doppler-processing kernels in C++ for the receiver’s processing board — a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ SoC — under a hard per-pulse timing constraint of 10 microseconds. The board’s limited on-chip memory required a streaming architecture that processed each range line in place before the next pulse arrived. Getting the FFT pipeline within budget while keeping numerical precision at low SNR meant several rounds of fixed-point scaling and cache-aware profiling against captured field data.

My training supports this directly. My MSc at Rheinmark TU Aachen was in Electrical Engineering, and my thesis on adaptive spatial filtering for narrowband interference suppression in array receivers gave me a grounding in the mathematics of array processing and spatial filtering that I have drawn on throughout my career. The programme’s emphasis on linear algebra and transform theory has proved equally lasting, and the balance of electromagnetic theory and statistical signal processing mapped closely onto the work I have done since.

Kaikuvaara’s scope — SAR payloads, scatterometer electronics, ground-segment processing — sits well within my experience at Nordkom, and the chance to bring nearly two decades of that experience into a team with a different platform heritage and customer base is something I would genuinely value. I would be happy to discuss how my background matches your current requirements.

Yours sincerely,
Camille Rossi

That kind of problem is what I find most rewarding.

The coursework in spectral analysis, detection theory, and waveform design has been the most durable asset across twenty years of practical radar engineering, more useful in hindsight than any specific tool or language. The thesis examined spectral methods for wideband communications, but the mathematical core transferred directly to the radar processing I went on to do at Fenno.

For the past ten years at Hallaharju Space Systems I have worked on the simulation and verification side of signal processing -- building MATLAB-based signal chain models, designing simulation test cases against system requirements, writing verification reports, and maintaining the test infrastructure that catches problems before they ship. I have spent the last twelve years at Baltic Sensor Networks in Turku building signal processing systems for underwater acoustics, and I think this role at Kaikuvaara is the right next step for reasons I want to explain properly rather than just listing keywords.

The core of my work at Baltic has been sonar array processing — specifically, towed-array beamforming for hydrophone arrays ranging from 32 to 128 elements. I designed the beamspace transform that Baltic's 128-element towed array currently runs in production, and published the underlying algorithm in JNAS in 2019. The processing problems are the same ones that come up in any array system: spatial covariance estimation, sidelobe control, computational load management on embedded hardware with hard real-time constraints. I wrote and maintain the embedded DSP library (C on TI C5535) that implements these algorithms, so I have lived with both the mathematics and the firmware side of array processing for a long time.

The reason I see Kaikuvaara as a natural fit is that the underlying signal processing discipline transfers across domains even when the physical medium does not. Sonar and radar array processing share the same linear-algebra core — steering vectors, covariance matrices, beampattern synthesis — and my thesis work at Oulujoki University covered the mathematical foundations I use daily. What changes is the propagation physics and the hardware interface, and those are learnable for someone with the right grounding.

On the software side, I should also mention that I wrote the production data-acquisition and processing pipeline for Baltic's harbour monitoring demonstrator entirely in Python — instrument control, real-time data ingestion from multiple channels, automated quality checks, and archival. What Kaikuvaara builds matters in a way that most engineering work does not. Remote-sensing instruments that fly on real missions and collect data about the Earth are products where the engineering quality directly determines whether a scientific objective is met or returns nothing useful. That is the kind of work I want to spend my career on, and it is the central reason I am writing to you.

I first became interested in remote sensing during my final year at Politecnico del Naviglio. A visiting lecturer gave a seminar on the engineering behind radar altimeter instruments for ocean monitoring, and one idea in particular stayed with me: that the performance specifications of a signal processing chain directly constrain the science the instrument can do, and an engineering shortcut in noise floor or dynamic range does not just cost performance but can eliminate an entire measurement capability. It is why I specifically sought out instrument companies after graduating.

I joined Tuulenkaari Satellite Systems in Oulu in early 2023, and the three years since have been a thorough introduction to instrument-level engineering. I have worked on signal chain design, link budget analysis, simulation, and bench-level RF characterisation of receiver assemblies. The test bench work has been the most instructive part: running network analyser measurements, chasing impedance mismatches, verifying that what the hardware actually does matches what the simulation said it would. That is where I have learned the most about what careful engineering requires in practice.

The work has also given me a clear sense of where I want to go next. Tuulenkaari’s current product scope covers a relatively narrow slice of the instrument-engineering space, and after three years I feel ready for a broader set of problems. The signal processing fundamentals transfer; what I need is exposure to different sensor types and signal regimes.

I hold Croatian citizenship and have full, unrestricted EU work authorisation. I relocated from Milan to Oulu to take the Tuulenkaari position and have been based here since. I have experience with satellite and airborne platforms, and the practical discipline of working to tight interface and performance specifications is something my current role has instilled.

What draws me to Kaikuvaara is the breadth of your instrument portfolio – SAR, scatterometer, optical payloads, different frequency bands and mission profiles. That is the variety I am looking for. Dear Hiring Team,

Kaikuvaara’s Senior Signal Processing Engineer posting caught my attention for two connected reasons: the technical fit and Oulu itself.

I have spent the past fourteen years at Sinikaari Optics, working on signal processing for optical and RF receiver systems. After completing my MSc in Electrical Engineering at Kallavesi I moved straight into the signal processing group, and the work since then has covered a wide range of what your listing describes. On the RF bench side, I run front-end calibration campaigns — network analyser sweeps, antenna pattern measurements, S-parameter characterisation — and have a solid feel for where the models stop matching the hardware. On the embedded side, I wrote the real-time DSP firmware in C++ for the LR-28 scanning receiver, and on the software side I maintain a production Python calibration toolchain that our test engineering team relies on every day.

The part of my work that has grown the most in recent years is the phased-array work: adaptive beamforming design on Sinikaari’s 64-element receive array, including null-steering algorithms and closed-loop validation against physical antenna-range data. Extending this kind of array work into an instrument context — where the processing chain faces constraints that terrestrial systems do not — is the direction I want to take.

What Sinikaari has not given me is the mission side. The instruments are terrestrial, the deployment is predictable, and the constraints are comparatively gentle. I have wanted to move toward instruments designed for harder operating environments, where the design margins are tighter and getting the signal processing wrong has real consequences.

I should also mention that over the years I have taken on responsibility for leading small engineering teams and coordinating across firmware, hardware, and test groups. I still think of myself as hands-on — I would rather debug a register-level timing fault myself than delegate it — but I am comfortable running a workstream and holding people to a schedule when the project calls for it. The ability to sit in a design review and understand both the analogue front end and the firmware is something I think matters particularly in instrument electronics.

On the Oulu question: I know the city from the SORA-3 field campaign in 2021, and I have kept up with the local engineering scene since then. I attended a Suvanto Oulu workshop last winter, and the concentration of RF, photonics, and sensor instrument work in the region is genuinely striking. There are not many places in Finland where you can have a conversation about array processing at a conference coffee table and find three other people who do it for a living. Relocating would not be a difficulty, and the engineering community there is part of what makes the move attractive.

I look forward to discussing how my background might fit what you are building.

Best regards,
Mei Rahman

Twenty-four years at Sinikaari Optics, most of them in Oulu. This is what I would bring to Kaikuvaara’s Senior Signal Processing Engineer role.

Twenty-plus years of hands-on signal processing work across RF, optical, and embedded platforms. The embedded C/C++ DSP code on the OPM-4000 and the production Python calibration pipeline I built are both still running in daily production, which says more than a list of keywords. The VIS-SAT spaceborne imager project gave me direct experience with payload-grade processing requirements — timing budgets, radiation tolerance margins, and the kind of verification discipline that comes with hardware you cannot service after launch.

Between 2018 and 2020 I worked on the digital beamforming chain for a customer’s 5G massive-MIMO base station test platform. This was a 64-antenna unit where we developed the full beamforming pipeline from spatial-multiplexing-layer design through weight computation and real-time application on an FPGA. The project also involved extensive over-the-air testing and performance validation against link-budget predictions. It was a departure from Sinikaari’s usual instrument work, but the spatial processing and real-time architecture problems are, I suspect, very close to what Kaikuvaara’s array-based instruments require.

I am already in Oulu. Sinikaari has been a good place to work, but after two decades the problems have become familiar and I am looking for a different set. Kaikuvaara’s focus on remote-sensing payload electronics — the SAR and scatterometer instruments in particular — is the kind of domain where my combination of optics background, embedded DSP experience, and RF bench practice would be put to genuine use rather than spread across product lines as it sometimes is now.

The RF measurement side of the role is also a good match. I have spent enough hours in front of a VNA to know when a measurement setup is lying to me, and that kind of bench instinct is not something you pick up quickly.

I am not looking for a management role. I want to stay close to the implementation work and the hardware.

The Senior Signal Processing Engineer role at Kaikuvaara sits at the intersection of several things I have been working toward, and I wanted to explain why I think it could be the right next step for me even though my profile is not the most obvious match.

My path into signal processing was indirect. I studied mechanical engineering at Limmat Institute of Technology Zurich, where my thesis involved vibration analysis and modal testing for a turbine-blade qualification rig. The signal processing techniques I used there — spectral analysis, windowing, sensor-data conditioning — turned out to be more interesting to me than the mechanical side, and after graduating in 2021 I deliberately looked for a role that would let me continue with that work. I found it at Sinikaari Optics in Finland, where I joined the instrument development group as a signal processing engineer in 2022.

At Sinikaari I have worked on the OPM-5000 optical measurement platform: system-level MATLAB simulations, test specification development, interface documentation, and hardware integration support. It is a structured, thorough engineering environment and I have learned a great deal about instrument development practice. I took parental leave in 2024–2025 and returned to the same group earlier this year.

What I want next is a role with more depth on the algorithm and implementation side. At Sinikaari I have been closer to verification and documentation than to core algorithm work, and I am ready to move toward harder implementation problems. Kaikuvaara’s focus on remote-sensing instrument electronics looks like the right setting for that — real signals, real hardware constraints, problems where the processing is the hard part rather than just a module in someone else’s design.

A few things that may not be obvious from the CV. I have some familiarity with Kalman filtering and estimation theory, and I have taken on team coordination and leadership responsibilities beyond my formal title. Neither is well reflected in the project list but both are part of what I bring. I recognise that this role asks for more depth than I currently have in several areas, but the mathematical foundations transfer well — linear algebra, spectral methods, optimisation — and what I lack in domain-specific experience I would expect to pick up in a hands-on setting.

On a practical note, my partner and I have already started looking at housing in Oulu. We have family connections in northern Finland and the relocation is something we are actively planning regardless of this particular role.

I would welcome the chance to discuss whether my background could develop in the direction Kaikuvaara needs.

Best regards,
Sofia Kovac

Dear hiring team at Kaikuvaara Oy,

For the last few years I've been trying to find my way back to hands-on embedded work. I've been at Meridian Defence Electronics in Oulu since 2007, and the first three years were the ones that defined what I actually want to do with my career. I came in as a junior engineer on the tactical radio product line, and my main task was writing the real-time noise-suppression module for the voice channel in C. The target was a TI TMS320C6748 DSP, the end-to-end latency budget was 4 ms including ADC and DAC overhead, and the algorithm had to fit within 60% of the DSP's cycle budget because the channel equaliser ran on the same core. I converted the floating-point MATLAB prototype to fixed-point, built the frame-based processing pipeline, and spent weeks debugging timing faults through JTAG and Code Composer Studio. That module shipped in 2010 and, as far as I know, it is still in the current production firmware.

After that project my role gradually shifted. Meridian is a small company and the work that needed doing was algorithm design and test automation rather than embedded implementation. I've spent the last decade maintaining the MATLAB simulation environment, designing interference-rejection algorithms for the narrowband voice channel, and building automated regression suites for the audio codec test bench. It's useful work and I'm good at it, but it's not where I want to spend the next decade.

Your senior signal processing engineer role caught my attention because it sits squarely in the embedded, hardware-close domain I've been missing. I am not going to claim that audio DSP for tactical radios and remote-sensing instrument electronics are the same thing — the application domains are clearly different, and I'd have a learning curve on the instrumentation side. What I do think transfers is the discipline of getting code to run correctly on real hardware under real constraints: fixed-point arithmetic, cycle budgets, timing verification, debugging on target. Those problems are portable even when the signals are not.

On the practical side, I have been in Oulu since 2007 and have no intention of leaving. My family is here, my life is here, and the prospect of working on something new without relocating is genuinely what makes this opportunity interesting.

I'd appreciate the chance to talk this through.

Riikka Turunen

Kaikuvaara came to my attention through the Oulu Electronics Forum last autumn, and the Senior Signal Processing Engineer posting looks like a genuine fit for the kind of work I do at Sumuvire Wireless.

Most of my career at Sumuvire has been hands-on RF measurement and signal chain work for their wireless infrastructure products — base station compliance testing, filter design, regression measurement campaigns against CTSI standards. It is not the most visible project at Sumuvire — the company is better known for its base station products than the embedded processing inside them — but it is the piece of work I am most satisfied with.

Oulu’s RF and photonics engineering cluster is one of the reasons I have stayed in this city as long as I have. I regularly attend Suvanto’s open-lab events, the Northern Radio Conference, and the occasional Oulu Systems Forum seminar. Through those I have come to know a reasonable number of engineers working in adjacent fields locally, and Kaikuvaara sits within that cluster. The prospect of bringing my measurement and signal processing skills into a different product domain is genuinely appealing.

I should be clear about the limitations. After more than two decades at a single employer, my experience is deep but narrow — Sumuvire’s LMR and PMR product families, primarily. I have not worked on the types of systems I expect Kaikuvaara builds. The core competences should transfer: RF measurement discipline, signal chain understanding from antenna port to baseband, comfort working close to hardware. But I recognise there would be a learning curve, and at this stage of my career that is a welcome prospect rather than a concern.

I would be glad to discuss whether my background is useful to your team. I can be reached at the details above and am available within a standard notice period.

To the Hiring Manager,

I have spent the better part of two decades in wireless signal processing at Sumuvire Wireless, and there are things about that work I still find genuinely interesting. But I have reached a point where I want the systems I contribute to to end up somewhere other than a base station or a handset. Kaikuvaara's focus on remote-sensing instrumentation is what caught my attention. The engineering constraints in mission-critical instrument design -- reliability budgets, calibration regimes, the basic fact that nobody can go out and reboot the hardware if something drifts -- are fundamentally different from consumer wireless, and that difference is the attraction.

In the last three years at Sumuvire I have been working specifically on phased-array beamforming algorithms for 5G NR massive MIMO base stations. The core of that project involved designing digital beamforming weight computations for a 64-element planar array, simulating beam patterns under various steering and interference conditions, and validating the beam steering performance against over-the-air measurements in Sumuvire's anechoic chamber. candidates.lt:
What drew me to the Senior Signal Processing Engineer opening at Kaikuvaara Oy was the measurement and characterisation angle that I gathered from the job description. My background is in RF measurement rather than algorithm development or system design, and I want to be upfront about that, but I think there may be enough overlap to make this worth a conversation.

I've been at Polaris RF Labs in Espoo for most of my career – since January 2014, with a sabbatical year in 2016–17. My day-to-day work is running antenna measurement campaigns. I handle everything from fixture design through to final reporting: setting up prototypes in the anechoic chamber, running S-parameter sweeps and pattern measurements on PNA-X and ZVA network analysers, processing the near-field data, and compiling the results into technical reports for customers. It's hands-on lab work and I've become very comfortable with it over the years.

My degree is in Industrial Management from Tammerkoski University, which I know is not the conventional background for this kind of role. The path was somewhat accidental – I did a summer placement at Polaris during my studies, helping set up measurement equipment in the lab, and they offered me a position after graduation. The RF measurement work turned out to suit me and I stuck with it. Over ten years I've built up practical knowledge that I couldn't have got from coursework, even if the theoretical foundations are something I've had to pick up along the way rather than study formally.

Since coming back from the sabbatical I've taken on more of the complex measurement campaigns – broadband prototypes where the fixture design needs custom work and the coupling paths are tricky to account for. Those projects have been the most educational. But at Polaris my responsibilities have stayed relatively static overall. It's a small lab team and the work is cyclical.

The sabbatical in 2016–17 was something I'd planned for a while. I spent eight months travelling through Thailand, Vietnam, and Laos, then three months in Peru and Bolivia. When I got back, I returned to the same role at Polaris and picked things up again fairly quickly. The fundamentals of the measurement work hadn't changed, though the lab had some new equipment that took time to learn.

I'm applying to Kaikuvaara because I'd like my next step to involve more than what I currently do. I don't have exposure to the broader signal processing challenges that Kaikuvaara seems to work on, and I'm realistic about the gap between what I do now and what this role probably requires. But I'm willing to learn, and the measurement side of things is one area where I could contribute from the start.

I hold a Finnish permanent residence permit and have been in Finland since 2013. I'm based in Espoo but would happily relocate to Oulu – I've moved before for work and have no particular ties to the capital region.

I've attached my CV and am available to discuss the role at your convenience.

Oulu's concentration of RF and photonics companies has caught my attention over the past few years. I think there is enough here to be worth a conversation, and I hope the application gives you enough to consider one.

candidates.lt:
After fourteen years at Meridian Defence Electronics, I'm looking for a change. Not because the work itself has gone stale – the HAR-6 programme I was on most recently was technically the best project of my career – but because Meridian's reorganisation has shifted the Stockholm DSP group away from new development and towards sustainment of delivered systems. I'd rather keep building things.

My background is array signal processing. I wrote my MSc thesis at RRIT on wideband spatial filtering, and everything I've done since at Meridian has been radar signal processing in one form or another – ground surveillance, airborne GMTI, electronic warfare support. What I've enjoyed most has been work where I follow a problem from initial algorithm design through embedded implementation into field validation.

Kaikuvaara's posting describes the kind of engineering environment I'm looking for: a phased-array-focused company, small enough that the distance between algorithm design and deployed hardware is short. At Meridian I've watched that distance grow as the organisation has layered programme management between the engineering teams and actual system integration. I don't want to spend the next decade writing reports about algorithms that someone else implements.

What I bring is fairly specific. I've designed and built adaptive beamformers, written embedded DSP firmware running in real time on multi-core processors, built production test infrastructure, and characterised RF hardware in chamber and field environments. I've done this across multiple radar programmes, on systems that have been delivered and are in operational use. The profile is narrow but deep.

What I don't bring: I have never worked outside defence. Defence customers operate on long cycles with heavy documentation overhead, and I have no idea whether that maps to Kaikuvaara's delivery model. I'd expect some adjustment period.

I also want to be direct about what I'm looking for. This isn't a speculative application. I've been thinking about leaving Meridian for the better part of a year, and the only openings that interest me are ones where phased-array signal processing is the core work. Kaikuvaara is one of a very small number of companies in the Nordics doing that at a serious level, which is why I'm writing.

If the profile looks like a plausible fit, I'm available to talk at your convenience.

candidates.lt:
I graduated from Tammerkoski University last year with an MSc in Electrical Engineering and have been working at Polaris RF Labs since January. That makes me junior for a senior position, I know, and I'm applying anyway because the technical fit between my experience and what Kaikuvaara does seems closer than my years of experience alone would suggest.

The specific overlap is in phased-array signal processing. At Polaris, the satellite communication terminal I work on uses a 16-element planar phased array for tracking LEO satellites across the sky. I've been responsible for the beam-steering implementation – computing pointing weights from orbital prediction data and applying them in real time during satellite passes. The accuracy requirements are tight because LEO pass durations are short and the handover between satellites needs to be seamless. Most of the algorithm work was prototyped in MATLAB, but the deployed version runs on a TI C6748 DSP, and I wrote the C implementation of the beam-steering controller including the weight computation loop and the SPI interface to the RF front-end module.

Oulu's RF and photonics engineering cluster has been on my radar since my thesis years at Tampere. Several companies in the region work on problems adjacent to satellite communication, but Kaikuvaara's focus on phased-array systems specifically is what sets it apart. I've been following the company for a while and the chance to work on larger, more complex arrays than the 16-element terminal I deal with at Polaris would be a genuine step forward technically.

One thing I can offer despite limited post-university experience is a track record of writing code that gets used. The Python test framework I built at Polaris runs every night and has caught real bugs. The embedded C code for the beam-steering controller runs in the field. I co-authored a paper that went through peer review and was presented at BALSIPCO. None of this is the scale of accomplishment you'd get from a candidate with ten years of experience, obviously, but it's real work and I think it shows I can deliver.

What I lack is breadth. I've been at one employer. The systems I've worked on are small compared to what Kaikuvaara probably builds, and I haven't been through a full product development cycle from requirements through to field deployment. I'd be bringing strong fundamentals in a narrow area rather than broad industrial experience.

Whether that's enough for a senior role is your call. I wouldn't normally apply for a position at this level, but the alignment between the phased-array and embedded DSP work I do now and what this role requires seemed too close to pass up without trying. If you're open to hearing from a less experienced candidate with directly relevant recent work, I'd appreciate the chance to speak with you.

PROJECTS

4-Element Beamforming Demonstrator (personal project, 2023)
Built a small phased-array beamforming setup at home using four microstrip patch antenna elements at 2.4 GHz on a custom PCB, with individual RF phase shifters controlled via an Arduino Mega. Implemented a delay-and-sum beamformer and measured the resulting patterns using a makeshift rotary positioner in my garage. Element spacing was set at half-wavelength based on first-principles calculations. Measured roughly 8 dB directional gain relative to a single element, with beam steering across about ±30 degrees before grating lobes became significant. The calibration process — compensating for element-to-element phase and amplitude mismatch — turned out to be the most difficult part and was done iteratively with a signal generator and oscilloscope. Not production-quality by any measure, but useful for building intuition about array calibration and weight computation.

MSc Thesis Work (Sakura National University, 2004–2005)
My master’s research in applied physics involved modelling RF wave propagation through urban geometries using FDTD methods. The simulation framework required validation against analytically solvable cases, which gave me a working understanding of electromagnetic field behaviour, antenna radiation characteristics, and numerical methods for wave equations. The physics and mathematics from this work have been directly applicable to the transceiver signal path design I’ve done at Sumuvire over the past two decades.

SKILLS

- Python: built automated production test scripts at Sumuvire for transceiver board-level validation (pytest, pySerial, NumPy); scripts run as part of manufacturing acceptance and are used on every board
- RF measurement: regular use of spectrum analysers (R&S FSW), signal generators (Keysight E8267D), and oscilloscopes for transceiver development, characterisation, and debugging
- Languages: English (working language at Sumuvire since 2010, when international customer contracts started), Finnish (intermediate), Japanese (conversational from university years)

candidates.lt:
I’ve lived in Oulu for twenty years now and have watched the RF engineering community here change shape — from what was mostly Korvenmaa legacy into something broader and more varied. Sumuvire Wireless has been a good employer through all of that, but the signal processing problems at a small transceiver company are bounded, and after nearly two decades I know where the ceiling is. Kaikuvaara works on things I haven’t been able to do at Sumuvire, and the fact that I wouldn’t need to uproot my life to take the job is a practical advantage worth stating plainly.

My career at Sumuvire has been long and narrowly focused. I joined in 2006 after finishing my MSc at the Sakura National University in applied physics, and the work has always centred on single-channel transceiver baseband processing — synchronisation, equalisation, receiver firmware. It’s solid work and I’m good at it, but the problems I solve now are refinements of problems I solved a decade ago.

What draws me to Kaikuvaara is the shift from single-channel to array-based systems. I’ve been curious about spatial signal processing for a while and have explored it on my own time — enough to appreciate how large the gap is between a hobby experiment and a production multi-element system. The real learning happens on the production side, and I’d like to be there.

I know the Oulu engineering ecosystem well. I attend Suvanto’s sensor workshops, I know people at several of the local companies, and I follow the work coming out of the university’s CRSR group. Kaikuvaara’s growth over the past few years has been visible from within the community, and the word is that you do genuine array work rather than consultancy. That matters.

The practical side is simple: I live here already, my family is here, and I have no interest in relocating. If the technical fit works, the logistics are trivial.

I should be honest about what might give you pause. Twenty years at one small company means depth in a narrow domain. My formal training is in applied physics, not electrical engineering, and the array work I’ve done is self-directed. Whether that profile is enough for what you need is a fair question, and I’d rather discuss it in person than argue it in a letter.

candidates.lt:
Signal processing for phased-array systems is where I want my career to go next, and that means leaving Kajanti Avionics.

I’ve spent fourteen years at Kajanti in Oulu doing sensor-level signal processing. The physics PhD gave me a strong foundation in statistical detection theory and spectral analysis, and I’ve applied those methods daily — designing detection algorithms, building analysis infrastructure, running characterisation campaigns. But the work has been overwhelmingly single-channel, and after this long the technical ceiling is real.

That changed earlier this year when I was brought onto a customer project involving a 32-element receive array for a ground-based surveillance application. I designed the digital beamforming pipeline from scratch: spatial covariance estimation, adaptive weight computation, beam pattern verification against predicted performance. I also built the array calibration procedure, mapping measured element patterns to steering vector corrections. Those eight months were the most technically demanding and engaging of my career at Kajanti, and they made it obvious that phased-array work is what I want as my main focus.

Kaikuvaara is the obvious next step. It’s the company in Oulu — in Finland, really — where array-based signal processing is core business rather than a sideline. Going from Kajanti, where array work surfaces as an occasional customer request, to somewhere it’s the daily work is exactly the shift I need.

I’m also comfortable with Kalman filtering and estimation theory, though my recent applied work has been mostly on the detection side.

My CV reads as weighted toward physics and sensor-level work, and it is. But the signal processing fundamentals carry across — spatial filtering, adaptive algorithms, calibration, embedded implementation — and the move from single-channel to array processing is one I’ve already started. I’d like to complete it at Kaikuvaara.

I’m in Oulu already. No relocation involved.

Oulu is not a city people end up in by accident. I moved here from Seoul in 2000 to take a position at Vireo Sensor Systems, and the reason I have stayed for twenty-six years is the concentration of RF and sensor engineering companies in this part of Finland. There are perhaps four or five places in Europe where you could spend a whole career working on precision sensor systems without relocating, and Oulu is one of them. Kaikuvaara is one of the companies that makes that true.

My MSc at Bukak National University was in electrical engineering, with a focus on antenna design and electromagnetic wave propagation. The programme had a strong laboratory component, and my thesis involved designing, calibrating and characterising the university's S-band ground station for the CubeSat programme we were running at the time. That work gave me practical experience with network analysers, antenna pattern measurements, and the discipline of producing repeatable measurements on hardware that is hard to modify once deployed. The combination of electromagnetic theory and hands-on measurement technique from those years has underpinned everything I have done since.

At Vireo, the work that best illustrates my capabilities is my most recent project: the beamforming processor for a next-generation maritime surveillance radar. The system uses a 24-element electronically scanned array, and I was responsible for the complete beamforming algorithm design, including per-element amplitude and phase calibration to meet the specified sidelobe performance. Aligning the measured element patterns with the predicted array factor was a three-month effort of iterating between antenna measurement data and the digital beamformer weights until the integrated system met specification. That project brought together my original training in antenna theory with two decades of DSP implementation experience, and it was the most satisfying engineering I have done at Vireo.

I should be straightforward about one limitation. My RF measurement experience is primarily from academic work rather than from a professional metrology environment. At Vireo the measurement campaigns have been handled by a dedicated test group, and my contribution has been on the algorithm and software side. Whether S-band ground station characterisation from the late 1990s constitutes current bench experience is a fair question, and I will not overstate it. The analytical framework -- understanding how antenna physics maps to signal processing performance -- is something I use daily, but the hands-on measurement skills are not recent.

My expectation is that the main learning curve at Kaikuvaara would be in the application physics rather than the engineering methods. Array calibration, real-time implementation, and systematic validation transfer across sensor types. I have moved between domains within Vireo before, and the adjustment has always been in the physics, not in the engineering discipline.

What draws me to Kaikuvaara beyond the work itself is how your organisation fits into Oulu's sensor engineering community. I know several of your engineers from Suvanto collaboration events and the local SESE section, and the quality of your instruments is well regarded here. I would welcome the chance to discuss how my background fits.

Sana Fernandez

Application for Senior Signal Processing Engineer – Kaikuvaara Oy

What first drew me to this listing was the kind of instruments Kaikuvaara builds. I have spent nearly twenty years doing RF measurements at Polaris RF Labs in Oulu, and while I find the work satisfying on its own terms, I have always been drawn to the question of what the components I measure actually end up doing – what systems they go into, what those systems are designed to see or detect. Nearly two decades at the same company has given me deep expertise in a narrow area, and I think the right time to broaden is now rather than later.

My most relevant experience for your needs is in phased-array antenna work. At Polaris, I spent two years between 2015 and 2017 performing element-level measurements on a 128-element L-band phased-array feed assembly for a client project. That included gain and phase calibration across the full array, mutual coupling characterisation between adjacent elements, and beam pattern verification against the client’s electromagnetic simulation models. It was the most technically demanding project I have worked on, and it gave me a real understanding of how array-level system performance depends on element-level measurement quality.

Most of my day-to-day work is at the component level – filters, low-noise amplifiers, individual antenna elements – using VNAs and spectrum analysers. All reporting and client documentation is in English, and I have been the primary measurement contact for several international accounts over the years. I have been at Polaris since 2006, with a break in 2008–2009 for postgraduate coursework in signal analysis methods, and I know the Oulu RF engineering community well by now. The measurement side of what I do is strong. What I lack is experience on the signal processing system design end – I have always been downstream of the design, verifying what others have built rather than building it myself. Moving towards system-level work is my main motivation for looking at this role.

Kaikuvaara’s focus on mission-critical instrumentation is genuinely compelling to me. The precision that goes into instruments that must work at their absolute limits, with no room for measurement drift or systematic error, is the kind of engineering I want to be closer to. My degree is in process engineering, not a signal processing field, and I will not pretend otherwise – but twenty years of hands-on RF measurement work has given me practical skills that speak for themselves.

I have been in Oulu since 2005 and intend to stay. If the profile seems a reasonable match, I would be happy to meet.

Rosa Li

My eight years at Vireo Sensor Systems have been focused on one thing: getting phased-array radar signal chains from prototype to fielded hardware. I am applying for the Senior Signal Processing Engineer role at Kaikuvaara because the scope of your systems and the environmental constraints you design for match what I want to work on next.

The most substantial deliverable from my time at Vireo is the digital beamforming pipeline for our 128-element L-band phased-array radar prototype. That campaign alone ran eight months and involved characterising every element feed, measuring the full array pattern in Vireo's near-field range, and diagnosing a systematic phase-taper error that simulation had not predicted. The root cause turned out to be a cable-routing issue inside the array housing that introduced a temperature-dependent path-length gradient. These are the kinds of problems I find most satisfying: the ones where theory meets hardware and the hardware wins.

I also built the automated post-processing pipeline in Python for our SAR image-formation chain. This system runs unattended on the customer's servers and has processed over 40 TB of raw data since 2021 without requiring manual intervention. I wrote the full chain from scratch -- ingestion, motion compensation, autofocus, image formation, and quality-metric extraction -- and it remains the production tool in daily use.

More recently I contributed to the signal processing subsystem for an airborne SAR demonstrator. Adapting our ground-based algorithms to cope with platform vibration, attitude uncertainty, and a reduced computational budget was a different kind of challenge, and one I found more interesting than I expected. The system was delivered on schedule and the customer has extended the contract for a second flight campaign.

On the theoretical side, I have solid experience with Kalman filtering and estimation theory, which I expect is relevant to the tracking and state-estimation problems in your domain.

I see Kaikuvaara's work as a step up in both complexity and consequence from what Vireo typically handles. The phased-array fundamentals are the same, but your operating environments demand harder constraints and narrower margins. That kind of engineering appeals to me. I would be glad to discuss specifics in an interview and can share technical details about the L-band system under NDA if useful.

candidates.lt:
When I moved from Germany to Oulu in 2018 to join Hallaharju Space Systems, the draw was purely technical: I wanted to work on phased arrays, and Hallaharju's ground-based monitoring systems used exactly the kind of dense receive arrays I had written my master's thesis on at RMTU. Eight years later, the job has delivered on that promise and then some.

My path into signal processing was through electromagnetics. At RMTU I studied antenna theory and EM field simulation, and my thesis dealt with mutual coupling compensation in dense arrays -- the gap between the ideal pattern and what you actually measure when 64 elements are packed into a tight aperture. At Hallaharju I have been able to apply that work directly, first in building the calibration methodology for our UHF receive array and then in the broader signal processing chain: beamforming, interference rejection, and the embedded firmware that runs it all.

The role at Hallaharju has been unusually broad for a single position. I write the DSP firmware, run the RF measurement campaigns when we bring up new hardware, maintain the test infrastructure, and handle the calibration data pipeline. That breadth is partly a consequence of being in a small team, but I have come to see it as a real strength in my profile. I have spent as much time at the bench with a VNA and probe fixtures as I have at a desk writing code, and I think that combination is what makes me effective at the system level rather than just in one slice of it.

The reason I am looking at Kaikuvaara is that I would like to do similar work with more resources behind it. Hallaharju is a good company but the team is small and the product line is narrow. After eight years I have worked on essentially one array architecture in depth. Kaikuvaara's scope suggests a wider variety of systems and, I would hope, more engineers to learn from and collaborate with. Oulu is where I live and want to continue living, so geography is not a factor in this decision.

I do not have a tidy narrative about climbing a career ladder, because that is not what the last eight years have looked like. What I do have is deep, hands-on experience in exactly the technical areas your role describes: phased-array processing, embedded firmware for real-time DSP, RF measurement and calibration, and the tooling that holds a development workflow together. Most of that experience has been acquired by being the person who has to figure something out because no one else on the team had done it before, which is perhaps not the worst way to learn.

I would be happy to discuss specific projects or go through technical details at your convenience.

Ingrid Andersson

candidates.lt:
After sixteen years building signal processing capability at Sinikaari Optics, I am looking for a position where I can apply the full scope of what I have learned. The Senior Signal Processing Engineer role at Kaikuvaara is that position.

My career at Sinikaari has taken me from pure algorithm development into the kind of hands-on system work that requires you to think across multiple engineering layers simultaneously. I started writing spectral analysis code for optical inspection and over the years expanded into embedded DSP implementation in C and C++, where I learned what it means to get algorithms running under real-time constraints on actual hardware rather than in simulation. I have also developed significant production Python capability – automated testing frameworks, batch processing pipelines, deployment scripts – which has become an increasingly large part of my daily work.

What I think distinguishes my profile is that these are not isolated competencies. I work across all of them in my day-to-day role, and I understand how they connect in a real engineering workflow. Too many engineers are specialists in one layer – they can design an algorithm but cannot debug a hardware integration, or they can write production code but have never characterised a signal chain end to end. I do all of it, routinely.

On the measurement side, I have built up practical experience in RF measurement and characterisation through years of working with real hardware and real signal chains. This is not something you acquire from textbooks. It comes from thousands of hours on a bench figuring out why the measured performance refuses to match the simulation.

My academic grounding is strong. The training I received has served me well throughout my career and I continue to build on it. I have also maintained a presence in the research community through technical publications and conference contributions, which keeps my thinking sharp and helps me evaluate new methods critically rather than just adopting whatever is fashionable.

There is a gap on my CV from October 2010 to late 2011 when I was recovering from a serious illness. I came back to Sinikaari and picked up where I left off. If anything, the experience gave me a clearer sense of what I want from a working environment and what kind of problems I want to spend my time solving.

What draws me to Kaikuvaara specifically is the level of technical difficulty your instrument work operates at. I have spent time working in the Oulu area on deployment projects and found the engineering environment there to be focused and serious in a way that suits me. The problems you solve demand someone who can move between theory and practice without losing rigour in either direction, and that is how I have built my career.

I look forward to discussing this further.

Camille Fischer

After 25 years at Boreal Photonics I am not looking for a change out of restlessness; I am looking for a context where the scope of problems matches what I can actually deliver.

My career at Boreal has been in photonic sensor systems, which is a domain that shares more with Kaikuvaara's work than it might appear on the surface. The core signal processing challenges – detection at low SNR, signal recovery in noisy and non-stationary environments, algorithm-hardware co-design – are fundamentally the same whether the sensor is optical or RF. What changes is the physics at the front end; the engineering behind it translates.

That combination of precision, reliability, and the physical reality of harsh operating environments is something I have always been drawn to.

On a practical note, I have been actively considering a move to Oulu for some time. My partner has family connections in the region and we have visited regularly over the past several years. candidates.lt:
Kaikuvaara's work on mission-critical remote-sensing instruments is the reason I am applying for this role rather than staying where I am comfortable. At Polaris RF Labs I have a stable position doing work I find interesting, but the prospect of contributing to instruments that operate on spaceborne and airborne platforms – where the engineering decisions made during development directly determine mission success – is something I have wanted to pursue for a long time.

My professional background is in RF receiver systems. For the past twelve years at Polaris I have worked on wideband receiver products, doing everything from RF characterisation on the bench to tracking loop algorithm design. One area where I have built particular depth is embedded DSP. A significant part of my work involves writing and optimising real-time signal processing code in C and C++ for TI DSP and ARM Cortex-M platforms – carrier acquisition loops, synchronisation engines, real-time spectral monitoring modules. These are not simulations running on a workstation; they run on hardware with fixed clock budgets and you find out quickly whether your approach actually holds up.

On the software tooling side, I have built and maintained several production Python tools that our engineering team relies on daily – automated test execution and reporting, measurement instrument control libraries, and a build verification framework that runs against our firmware every night. These are not throwaway scripts; they are versioned, tested, documented, and other engineers depend on them. Building that kind of infrastructure is not the most visible part of the job but I believe it is one of the most impactful. When your test tooling is solid, the whole team catches regressions earlier, which matters enormously in a product cycle where late-found bugs are expensive.

I should note that Polaris RF Labs is an English-speaking workplace. Our team includes engineers from Finland, Hungary, Germany, India, and the UK, and all technical communication – design reviews, documentation, daily coordination, everything – happens in English. I have worked in this environment for my entire career and it is completely natural.

What draws me to Kaikuvaara specifically is the integration challenge that mission-critical instruments present. In my experience, the hardest engineering problems sit at the interfaces: between algorithm and hardware, between simulation and measurement, between what the spec promises and what the physics delivers. Instruments that operate on remote platforms add another dimension – they must work without intervention, in harsh environments, under constrained resources. I find that combination deeply motivating.

I am based in Helsinki but have already been looking at Oulu as a place to move, for both professional and personal reasons. I would welcome the chance to discuss this role with you.

Matteo Horvath
